opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
There are many parallels in today’s readings. They feel like multiple stories happening at once, except they are not separate stories at all. What is being revealed is that the Exodus is not merely history — it becomes a pattern. The same story unfolds at different points in time.

In Deuteronomy, the Israelites are finally free. Yet immediately after liberation comes hunger. At first, that feels unfair. They leave oppression only to enter testing. But Moses tells them something uncomfortable: God allowed hunger, affliction, and dependence so they would learn that human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.

The manna itself becomes strange because it is more than food. It is dependence made visible. Every morning, they must trust again. Every morning they must gather again. They cannot store enough certainty for tomorrow.

Then the readings begin to overlap.

The manna was unknown to their ancestors. Yet in the Gospel, Jesus says, “Your ancestors ate manna and died.” That sounds harsh until we realize He is not criticizing manna. He is completing it. The manna kept Israel alive physically during an arduous journey. Christ says He becomes bread for the deeper journey. The first bread sustained life. The second bread gives life.

This raises an important question. Was the manna a foreshadowing of Christ? Christian tradition has long understood it this way. The manna points forward to the Bread of Life and ultimately to the Eucharist.

The pattern begins to emerge. Egypt is slavery. The Exodus is liberation. The desert is testing. Manna is sustenance. The Promised Land is the destination.

Then comes Christ. Sin becomes slavery. Christ becomes liberation. Life becomes a desert of testing. The Eucharist becomes sustenance. Eternal life becomes a destination.

As I reread these passages, another question arises. Did those who ate manna receive everlasting life? Eating manna itself did not save them, just as receiving the sacraments mechanically is not Christianity. Relationship with God matters. Faith matters. Our response matters.

In John’s Gospel, Jesus presents Himself not as an optional enrichment, but as necessary nourishment. And just as it was for Israel, the desert never fully disappears. We simply inhabit different deserts. The Israelites struggled despite plagues, parted seas, manna, fire, and miracles. Visible miracles alone did not guarantee belief. Human beings still wrestle, still doubt, still complain, and still hunger.

The Exodus is constantly happening. People are continually leaving Egypt — addictions, grief, pride, loneliness, fear, false identities, and suffering. And in these deserts, bread matters.

The manna is Christ present among us today. The manna appeared every morning, not once, but daily. In the same way, Christ gives Himself not as a memory of something long ago, but as continuing sustenance for the journey.

The Exodus continues. The desert continues. And the bread continues too.
